entry.title: Our Favorite Montessori-Style Tools for Cooking With Kids
entry.summary: All the prep tools, furniture, tableware, and more we’ve used successfully with children at home and in the classroom.
entry.content:
We love cooking with children — even (maybe especially!) with very young, unpredictable toddlers — and we believe that any parent can, too. We also know that in every egg messily cracked, carrot scrubbed, and cookie rolled, there are huge benefits, not just to children but to parents and the connection between them.

Though we’re both raising young children ourselves, our careers have been quite different: Junnifa is an AMI-trained Montessori teacher; the founder of Fruitful Orchard Montessori in Abuja, Nigeria; and the co-author of the best-selling The Parents’ Guide to Montessori series; Kristen is the author behind Food52’s Genius Recipes cookbook series living in the San Francisco Bay Area. But the best parts of our days overlap where our work comes together: cooking alongside little ones.

We’ve heard so many times from parents who want to bring their children into the kitchen but either find the potential for mess and chaos stressful, don’t think they have the time, or just aren’t sure where to begin. So we teamed up to write The Montessori Kitchen, a cookbook-meets-parenting guide with lots of pep talks, simple recipes, and activities for parents to connect with their children in the kitchen at each stage of development from pregnancy through age 6 and beyond.

Because, with some simple mind-set shifts and a better understanding of what will engage and thrill children at various ages, sharing the kitchen with even the youngest ones can look very different: It can turn into a place of discovery and growth, helping them strengthen everything from fine motor skills to language and math concepts to patience and resilience — all from sorting through beans and waiting for the oven to beep!

Having a handful of accessible, child-size tools to welcome them in and bring order and predictability to the kitchen can also make a world of difference. Below are the tools that we’ve seen work best for small hands and bodies, both at home and in the classroom, and have made the kitchen the most rewarding place for us to parent.

A sturdy learning tower acts just like a wooden chair pulled up to the counter, giving little ones access to the same cooking surface as you, with a little more structure and peace of mind. This one has a small footprint, even tucking underneath the counter, and as your child grows you can adjust the height (and they can use the low handles to start dragging it from the sink to the fridge to the high cereal cabinet).

In Montessori classrooms, aprons aren’t just used for messier projects but each time children cook, as a marker to let them know the beginning and end of the process. Junnifa likes to start her youngest students with aprons like these that close with a Velcro strip, then move on to snaps, hooks, buttons, and finally ties as they get older and work on each skill. She also offers them two-sided aprons to begin the cooking process with an empowering choice. (Would you like the elephants or the flowers today?)

Simple baking recipes like cookies and quick breads are a good place to start cooking together, since measuring and mixing can usually happen at any pace, away from heat and sharp objects. Baking also casually introduces math, science, and literacy from an early age. These measuring cups reinforce fractions visually and really drive home the whole half-cup, quarter-cup concept.

Young children don’t quite have an understanding of time yet. Visual timers — a sand or fraction timer — help them quantify what is still an abstract idea and build patience. They can watch the sand, the liquid, or the size of the fraction gradually reduce until it is time to take out the tea bag or knead the dough.

While some tools already in your kitchen might fit comfortably in a child’s hands, look out for the ones that are unwieldy or frustrating for them to maneuver. Invest in a few just-their-size versions, like this masher that can squish not just potatoes but guacamole, refried beans, banana-bread batter, fruit compotes, and applesauce, too.

High-reward unitaskers like egg slicers and apple cutters are worth the drawer space. They build concentration and offer simple, repeatable processes to engage a child (mesmerize them, really), all while building hand strength and dexterity. This orange juicer is especially good for toddlers and young children who are in a period where they want to exert maximum effort and see the results.

It may feel instinctual to give a child a blunt knife, but it can actually be more dangerous because they end up using more force. Junnifa likes to progress children through a series of crinkle cutters that they can first use with two hands working together (the Tellashun), then one hand (the Joie), then two hands working separately as a sort of pre-knife.

She also likes a spreader with a serrated edge that can go beyond smearing PB&Js to double as a first knife for slicing soft foods like tomatoes and mozzarella. Choose what action best fits your child’s level (or try a few), always observing to make sure they’re using them safely.

A low table and chairs — also called a weaning table and chairs — are a big part of the Montessori philosophy to encourage eating independently but are also useful as food-prep surfaces and for drawing, writing, and countless craft projects. Because this table is designed to grow with children, Junnifa was able to use the same one for all four of hers. Her daughters still have it in their room as a work table.

This weaning chair allows children to sit with feet flat on the floor — important for safe self-feeding — and is stable but light enough that a child can start moving it themselves very early. They also make great step stools. Junnifa has lent them to extended family members when they had babies for 13 years and counting.

Famously and controversially, Montessori schools use real glasses and ceramic dishes, even in younger classrooms. They choose materials that won’t shatter but instead break into a few pieces. The children naturally learn from the consequence, unlike with bouncy silicone and plastic plates.

Instead of pouring water directly into children’s cups at mealtime, teachers set out small pitchers that little ones can manage themselves to refill their own cups again and again. Over time, they hone the skills of pouring and self-control as they learn to stop before the cup runs over. Outside mealtime, teachers also leave out small cups and a water dispenser at an accessible height, with a bowl or basin on the floor to catch drips (and mark the spot where children should hold the cup).

Bowls or plates with raised sides, rather than flat plates, are easier for small children to scoop against. Ramekins, which don’t shatter and are heavy enough that they don’t easily slide around, are good options for eating and serving, too.

Real silverware, sized for small hands, communicates respect and the feel of its weight invites care.

Meals in Montessori classrooms are served family-style with serving bowls and utensils that children can use successfully. They learn to identify how much they can eat and practice passing the bowl and returning the serving spoon or tongs to the dish (without licking them first).

Placemats with every utensil clearly marked serve as a cue that it’s time to eat and allow children to participate meaningfully at home by learning how to set the table for everyone, all through what is essentially a matching game.

We often think of the functional parts of eating, but young children are absorbing everything, including beauty and detail. Fresh flowers picked during a walk together and tucked into a small vase or a piece of art hung at their eye level can be a lovely, special part of meals.

When you open up the world of measuring and stirring and pouring (and the growing independence that comes along with it), messes will happen. Provide tools for cleaning up — like small dustpans, plenty of absorbent cloths, and adjustable mops (skip the disposable cloths and use a small towel) — and don’t make a big deal about it, and you’re indirectly teaching how to deal with the hard messes of life. You just clean up!

entry.title: I Found the Comfiest Socks for All Types of Boots
entry.summary: How to solve the problem of socks that scrunch up.
entry.content:
In our advice column, “Ask the Strategist,” we take your most burning shopping questions and survey friends, call up experts, and draw on our own personal experience to answer them. If you have an online-shopping question of your own, please send it to strategist@nymag.com with the subject “Ask the Strategist.” We’re here to help.

I get it. In the winter, like many city dwellers, I live in Blundstones. They’re bar none the most comfortable pair of shoes I own, but wear them with the wrong socks and suddenly they become the worst. A standard multipack of crew socks isn’t going to cut it; you’re going to spend all day tugging to keep them from bunching up in the heel. You need socks that hug your feet without feeling constrictive, and the more breathable the better. Styles like Blundstones require something more utilitarian, while dressier boots feel and look better with thinner, daintier socks. Below, the best socks for all types of (non-hiking) boots, from ankle socks to knee-highs, including ones you hide in your shoes and others you want to show off.

The socks I look for first are from Paka. They are made of 40 percent baby-alpaca fiber, 8 percent Tencel, 50 percent polyester, and 2 percent spandex. They are soft and durable and feel nice and fitted on my feet thanks to the ribbed arch support. They have a cushioned sole and toe but never feel too thick or bulky and are still so warm and breathable. I’ve owned a version of the brand’s Essential Crew Socks for 19 months, and they’re still going strong with no visible wearing out at the heel or anywhere else.

I also love my Smartwool socks. I’ve had a pair of the Everyday Margarita for over five years, and they have held up beautifully. Their composition is 52 percent merino wool, 44 percent nylon, and 4 percent elastane, and they have a similar feel, though they are not cushioned. These socks are thinner and not as padded as the Paka and feel less soft, but they are another durable option. In general, alpaca is warmer than merino, so I might choose the Pakas over the Smartwools in very cold temperatures, but I honestly couldn’t tell you the difference in warmth.

My fellow Strategist senior writers Liza Corsillo and Michael Zhao both recommend Darn Tough socks for wearing with their everyday boots. Like the Smartwool, they are made with merino wool, nylon, and elastane. Corsillo likes the basic lifestyle socks — which don’t come with cushioning but have arch support — for being “not bulky” and wears them with her Blundstones and lace-up combat boots from Sézane.

Zhao likes wearing the mid-calf cushioned lightweight socks from Darn Tough with a dressier boot from R.M.Williams or Viberg Navvy. Unlike the basic Lifestyles above, these have cushioning in the sole and below the heel as well as arch support. (Zhao says these socks are “a bit too thick to be real dress socks in dress shoes, but they are perfect for wearing with a dressier boot.”)

Corsillo says her Darn Toughs are not necessarily worn to be seen. When she does want her socks to show, she opts for Uniqlo’s men’s Colorful 50 socks. They stay on and come in, as the product name suggests, 50 different colors. Made with a cotton blend, the combination of acrylic, polyester, nylon, and spandex varies on the color.

When I’m not wearing merino wool or alpaca socks, I usually just go with cotton socks. My favorites to wear with my Blundstones are ones from Aritzia and Le Bon Shoppe. Aritzia’s ankle socks are made with 80 percent cotton, have ribbed cuffs, and are nice and thick. They hug my feet and always stay on. (Aritzia’s TNA crew socks are another Strategist favorite.)

I have both the boyfriend (crew) and girlfriend (ankle) styles and love how thick and plush they are. Made with 85 percent cotton, they have built-in arch support, a breathable-mesh top-of-the-foot part, and a ribbed cuff with retro stripes. They also come in dozens of bright colors.

Zhao also recommends these socks from Falke. He loves the ankle-height version for everyday, but for boots, he suggests trying the knee-highs. “They are as richly colored as any cotton sock, but the added merino for moisture management is particularly useful for leather boots,” he says. Zhao calls them “a fancier, more comfortable Uniqlo 50 sock” that also comes in dozens of colors. He says they’re great for non-winter boots, as they are really light and “easy to fit into a dress shoe of any kind, even loafers.” They are made with merino wool on the outside and cotton on the inside.

For dressier boots that fit closer to the foot, like my patent-leather boots from Loq or combat boots from Church’s, I need a thinner sock. These crew socks from Uniqlo are made with polyester, nylon, and spandex and feel more like tights material. They have a thicker cuff that ensures the socks stay on — and prevents the opening of ankle boots from rubbing against your skin. I can wear these with loafers and brogues too.

I wear these longer crew socks from Hue a lot as well. They are made of a polyester, rayon, and spandex blend and feel a little slippier than cotton and wool socks (similar to the Uniqlo socks above) — that helps with boots that are tighter and have less give. Sometimes I’ll wear these over tights as added cushioning and protection with dressier or heeled boots.

Strategist writer Brenley Goertzen, who recently tested a bunch of tall riding boots, prefers wearing Maggie’s Organics crew socks, which are also the Strategist’s Best in Class pick for women’s white socks. “I love them since they are thicker and prevent my feet from getting blisters,” she says. She usually wears these socks over leggings or under jeans, then boots over that. Goertzen recommends getting them in a darker color so the boot doesn’t stain them. They are made with 98 percent organic cotton that has some stretch and are plush with a ribbed cuff that keeps them in place.

I recently tried these boot socks from Hue and was pleased with them when I wore them with my 16-inch Durango Crush western boots. Those boots have a pointed toe and a 2.5-inch heel, so I was worried about wearing socks that were too thick, but both the Bubbled style and the pointelle socks worked well. The bubbled style (made of mostly polyester) feels like a cozy, fuzzy sock — really soft and plush — but not too thick. They stay up surprisingly well and were good for the breaking-in period with the cowboy boots, which are on the stiffer side, and were not noticeably sweaty. I don’t have notes on durability yet, but if my other Hue socks are any indication as to quality, I am not worried about them.

The pointelle socks are thinner and have more breathability thanks to the composition of the material (58 polyester, 26 acrylic, 12 nylon, and 4 wool) and the stitching in the cuff. They also worked well with the Durangos, staying up with no bunching. I would choose these for looks if I were to wear them with lower boots.

I would try these with my riding boots. They are they knee-high version of Corsillo’s crew socks above and come in a couple of netural colors. I liked the ribbed design that makes them look preppy (and could work well with loafers too).

Next on my to-try list are these wool-and-cashmere socks from Calzedonia. I have a couple of pairs of crew socks in this blend that I wear with dressier shoes, and I imagine the knee-high length would be great for tall boots as well.

entry.title: The Best Gifts for 2-Year-Olds
entry.summary: Building toys, art supplies, dress-up clothes, and everything else you need to nurture their growing imagination and independence.
entry.content:
At age 2, toddlers are getting their first whiffs of independence and develping pride in their own abilities. Whether it’s figuring out how to ride a balance bike or putting together a simple puzzle, there’s a lot of “Look what I can do” energy. So the kind of play they are interested in at this age, according to Jeannette Corey, the director of the Bank Street Family Center, often focuses on the ways they can have an impact, accomplish a goal, or solve a problem, like feeding a baby doll who needs its bottle.

Two-year-olds are also practicing their language skills and learning how to socialize, often through pretend play, which “encourages children to interact with one another and share ideas,” says Hannah Lawton, the educational director at Park Slope Little Learners. To encourage this behavior, experts recommend toys that let children imagine themselves in the roles of adults and other important people in their lives, from a play kitchen where they can bake a make-believe cake to a doll stroller they can push to the park.

To curate this list of the best gifts for 2-year-olds, I relied on my experience as a mom who writes about toys for a living and talked to professionals like Corey and Lawton, as well as tasteful parents, toy-store owners, and teachers, about the toys they love and recommend. I organized everything by price so you can browse according to your budget, whether you want to spend $10 on a day-care buddy’s birthday or $150 on your only grandchild. And if you’re also shopping for kids of other ages, the Strategist has gift guides for 1-year-olds, 3-year-olds, 4-year-olds, 5-year-olds, 6-year-olds, 7-year-olds, 8-year-olds, 9-year-olds, 10-year-olds, 11-year-olds, and 12-year-olds — plus the Strategist Toy Hall of Fame filled with all of our greatest hits.

Updated October 26, 2026
I added several new picks and confirmed the pricing and availabity of all the gifts we recommend.

While pregnant with her second child, preschool teacher Kathleen Cann got a baby doll and a toy stroller for her then-2-year-old as a way to prepare for the arrival of a new sibling. “She was obsessed and took really sweet care of the doll,” says Cann. This umbrella-style stroller is a favorite toy of Strategist senior writer Lauren Ro, whose younger son (now 4) got one for his second birthday and still plays with it. It is easy to push and refreshingly gender neutral, folds up for storage, and has a real working canopy, plus a storage basket in the back.

Fisher-Price’s medical kit was so helpful when my son was 2 and feeling nervous about real-life doctor visits. He was fascinated with the syringe that has a real working plunger, loved pushing the button on the “digital” thermometer, and the included tote bag let him practice putting all his tools away. This kind of pretend play (combined with reading a Daniel Tiger book recommended to me by Strategist senior editor Winnie Yang) made him a lot more comfortable when it was time for the real thing.

But if you’re looking for more of a doctor dress-up toy, Kelly Harris Smith, founder of the Minni art space for kids in Boston, recommends a simple coat-and-stethoscope set from Learning Resources, as this type of imaginative play encourages toddlers’ empathy and imagination. Or Gigglescape, Target’s in house toy brand, makes a doctor play set specifically designed for use with 14-inch dolls for patients.

I discovered Fancy Pals, a line of stuffed animals sold inside adorable matching plush purses, while visiting a favorite toy store in Essex, Connecticut, with my mother. They are silly and adorable and, according to the shop owner, very popular. I bought a pony inside a cowboy-boot-shaped purse for a friend’s almost 2-year-old and considered buying another one (a unicorn inside a butterfly purse) just to keep on hand for the future. Like the doll stroller above, these purses let toddlers practice independence and empathy, toting their pets along on errands just like a grown-up would do.

There are an infinite number of construction-, garbage-, and fire-truck toys made for little kids. But this dump truck comes with a smiling driver you can take out and move around, and the bucket has a hinged gate that makes it easy to empty piles of dirt or sand. Plus it’s cheap enough that it won’t hurt too much to replace if it gets left at the playground or on the beach.

DUPLOs — LEGO’s larger blocks designed with smaller hands (and curious mouths) in mind — are great for 2-year-olds. And many kids continue to play with them as they get older, including my own son, who’s now almost 4 years old. The classic brick box is a fantastic gift, and many of the themed sets are affordable enough to give as add-ons.

After turning 2, my son became increasingly interested in puzzles. The sweet spot was around a dozen pieces, which made them challenging enough to hold his interest but didn’t take him longer than five to ten minutes to complete. Some of our favorites were the “pouch puzzles” from Mudpuppy, which I often packed on weekend trips.

This adorable push-button wooden telephone is a fun way to spark conversations between toddlers and their parents, grandparents, or siblings. It also makes it a little easier to say no when they ask to play with your smartphone.

Corey recommends giving balls to 2-year-olds because the toy will “grow” along with them: “Two-year-olds can roll them and chase them,” she says. “At around age 3, children can practice throwing and catching, while at 4, they might create a game with rules that involve a ball.” My son is drawn to balls of all kinds, but when he had just turned 2, his favorites were small enough for him to hold in one hand, like this owl soccer ball that we kept in the bottom of our stroller for over a year.

Sculpting with Play-Doh at this early age is similar to drawing; while they may not make especially impressive “art,” 2-year-olds are excited by the simple fact that they can manipulate the material. And it’s a good workout too. “Play-Doh builds dexterity in their hands and finger muscles,” explains Dr. Kathy Hirsh-Pasek, a professor of psychology at Temple University and co-author of Becoming Brilliant: What Science Tells Us About Raising Successful Children. This is also an important precursor for learning to write.

Here’s a set of easy-to-grip patternmakers for pressing into the Play-Doh. Each one makes a different animal print, from zebra stripes to fish scales.

One of the very first non-crayon art supplies I bought for my son was a set of these dot markers. They’re similar to bingo daubers in that they are full of liquid pigments and have a stamplike tip. But they are also washable, making them great for toddlers. Ali Brunson even included them on a list of things her daughter can’t live without.

This Ikea kids’ easel comes with a dowel to add a roll of paper, and the large surface area and short legs make it easy for 2-year-olds to reach. Rebeca Raney, an artist and arts educator, says “every nursery school has multiples of this one,” noting that “Ikea does a super job with their art products.” When you’re not using paper with it, kids can draw with dry-erase markers on one side and chalk on the other.

As they explore their growing independence, many 2-year-olds start asking for everyday tools and accessories of their own. Not only is this toddler-size umbrella from Original Duckhead fun to use, it will help them practice gross motor skills like walking while holding something above their head.

Melissa & Doug’s set of well-made cleaning tools is a perennial Strategist best-seller that I have seen entertain children for years — even if they stop sweeping and start using the broom as a sword or the mast of a cardboard-box pirate ship.

Strategist lead editor and parent of three Lauren Levy recommends Blockaroo’s magnetic foam blocks for kids this age; where Magna-Tiles are flat and have more of a learning curve, Blockaroo’s 3-D foam shapes are easier and less frustrating for younger kids to work with. They are also lightweight and soft and float in the bath.

I try to limit screen time for my son, but he adores playing with his Story Dream Machine, a retro-looking projector and audio player that we got as a baby step toward letting him watch TV. It’s basically a mini slide projector that plays read-aloud books, from Elmo’s Trip to the Dentist to Eric Carle classics. It has a convenient carry handle, a focus adjuster, and can be used as a nightlight and sound machine come bedtime. There are hundreds of titles for it, too, but this bundle comes with a trio of nostalgic Golden books.

Read more: This Retro Picture-Book Projector Is a Toddler Screen Alternative

Kids love looking at books with photographs of everyday people, especially other kids. Lovevery makes the best examples of this kind of board book that I have found. Like the brand’s toy kits, its books are curated in bundles by age with developmentally appropriate stories. My son loved this set because it includes a book about a fire station, with pictures of fire trucks that have flaps he could open to see inside every compartment and door.

Full-size dollhouses take up a lot of space and aren’t ideal for families with small apartments. Instead, Alexis Swerdloff, New York deputy editor and mom of two, suggests giving a more portable dollhouse like this one that closes up when it’s not in use. It comes in a few different designs, including this horse stable, a wooden barn, and a pink cottage.

This elaborate Melissa & Doug ice-cream-counter set combines fine-motor-skill development with elements of pretend play. “It almost always elicits conversation, negotiation, and turn-taking,” says Lawton, adding that it’s one of the most popular toys at her day care and preschool.

Meanwhile, the most popular toy in our pediatrician’s waiting room when my son was 2 was a simple pretend coffee maker. He got so much joy out of playing barista that I think it’s worth splurging on this detailed wooden set over cheaper plastic alternatives.

A first train set is a powerful memory for every generation, and Brio is the gold standard. All Brio sets can be endlessly expanded with accessories and integrated into play with other kits, even many from other brands. This is a wonderful starter kit that’s specifically designed for toddlers.

For younger kids who are just getting started with dolls, Emily Motayed Lancaster, co-founder of Nurture& and mom of two, recommends American Girl’s Bitty Baby line. She bought one when her own daughter was 2, and as with full-size American Girl dolls, there are many skin and hair colors available plus an entire Bitty Baby universe that includes furniture, clothing, a car seat, a baby carrier, and even a cup of peas and a snack pouch.

Yang strongly believes in giving kids real musical instruments as early as possible because they sound better than toy versions and help kids learn to treat belongings with care. She recommends this Kala ukulele for 2-year-olds because of the good sound quality and small size. Her daughter started playing with it as a toddler and later passed it down to her younger brother, who at age 2 loved to walk around strumming it.

Ride-on toys, like this miniature excavator with a kid-powered scoop, help toddlers practice gross motor skills while pretending to be all kinds of adults with different jobs. While it’s ideal for use in a sandbox, it will also get lots of use indoors digging and scooping up imaginary dirt and gravel.

Bouncing engages almost every muscle group in a child’s body, especially the legs and core, according to Lily Balsen, a New York City–based yoga teacher whose clients range in age from newborn to 80. So a classic toy like this Little Tikes trampoline will foster balance and a sense of spatial orientation, she says, adding that rhythmic movement is a great self-soothing and self-regulating mechanism. My son still loves bouncing on a similar mini-trampoline with a handlebar in my apartment building’s basement playroom. In fact, it is so popular kids will wait in line for a turn.

Strategist contributor Steven John has watched kids line up over and over for a chance to zoom down the track of this toddler-size ride-on roller coaster. And as long as a parent is nearby with a watchful eye, it’s perfectly safe for most 2-year-olds to use. Steps on either side of the platform let toddlers get on the car all by themselves — and it is just as fun to ride on level ground for youngsters who aren’t ready for the roller-coaster experience.

As an almost 2-year-old, my son would sit down on anything around the same height as his butt, backing up into a bottom step, his Nugget play couch, or a step stool and then proudly looking up at me once seated. So for his 2nd birthday, we got him a chair from Piccalio that goes from seat to step stool to activity table with a few turns. If we had more space in our apartment, I would have purchased this full set of two chairs and a table so he could sit and draw or eat with a friend.

The Woom GO 1 is our top-pick balance bike for its lightweight aluminum frame, low crossbar, shock-absorbing air-filled tires, and extra safety features. And according to Yang, it’s an ideal size for average-height children just turning 2. She prefers it for this age compared to the bigger Strider bike that her daughter started riding at age 4. Both bikes have 12-inch wheels, but the Woom’s crossbar curves down low to make it easier for shorter kids to get on.

Lawton says a play kitchen is a great addition to any 2-year-old’s space, noting that her students love to “cook” and share food with their classmates and teachers. Play kitchens come in all shapes and sizes, but Lovevery’s version stands out thanks to its real working sink. It’s a favorite of cookbook author and recipe developer Anna Jones, who bought one for her son when he was 2 years old. To make the spigot work, you fill a tank over the sink with water and turning the tap lets it slowly flow into a basin below. It comes with accessories like a cutting board, measuring cups, a wooden knife, a colander, and a tea towel, and Jones has added some real utensils as well. “My son chops real food when I am cooking or for a snack and washes his hands in the sink. The kitchen is an extension of our real kitchen,” she says. There is also a new slightly more expensive limited-edition version that Lovevery made in collaboration with cookware brand Our Place, which comes with a toddler-size skillet and wooden spatula.

entry.title: I Found Tall Riding Boots For Non–Horse Girls
entry.summary: They needed to have a supportive footbed that wouldn’t flare up my plantar fasciitis.
entry.content:
I’m not a horse girl (I wish!), but I’ve long loved the right-from-the-stables look that’s everywhere from Frye and Ralph Lauren to Barbour. It all makes me think of a pair of knee-high riding boots I sadly donated years ago. To fill this gap in my closet, I began hunting for a tall, tailored pair that embodied the spirit of lifelong equestrienne Jackie Kennedy Onassis — no horse necessary. But the main caveat was that they needed to be under $350. If you’ve shopped for boots of any kind lately, you’ll know that this is no easy feat. Lands’ End sells a nice-looking pair, and I had my eye on ones from Madewell, Sézane, and Dolce Vita. My ideal riding boots needed to be low-heeled — one to 1.5 inches — which is consistent with the real thing, which have a small heel that helps keep your foot in the stirrup. I wanted a supportive footbed that wouldn’t flare up my plantar fasciitis and a subtly rounded or almond-shaped toe. Finally, they should hit just under the knee, and hardware such as buckles and zippers wasn’t essential, but I didn’t mind it either.

These are waterproof, which is a win, but the grooves and stitching detailing around the outsole felt edgier than I wanted. The heel is around 1.2 inches, which is right around the sweet spot, but the blocky shape of the heel felt off to me. I think these are a solid pick if you want black boots that don’t necessarily have an obvious equestrian look, but I felt there might be a better option out there for me.

These are a pull-on style, which I actually didn’t mind. But beware: The shaft is snug and doesn’t have much give. I tested out the dark hickory leather color, which has a genuine calf-hair upper and a leather rounded toe. I absolutely loved the contrasting materials — the calf hair felt warm for cold weather and the textural shaft was insulting and soft. But for a classic riding boot that can transition through more than just fall and winter, I think I would have opted for the brand’s standard black leather finish.

From ballet flats to sandals and loafers, Madewell’s reasonably priced, all-leather shoes regularly get written up around here. The leather quality was the first thing I noticed about these, plus the very classic silhouette, which included a straight shaft and rounded toe. While the sole felt plenty cushy, the upper part of the boot was a different story; I have narrower feet, and the heel and mid-foot still felt snug. I imagine the leather will stretch out as I continue to break them in, but for those reasons, I decided to keep looking.

The Bridget boots from Sézane have a roughly 1.6-inch heel, but they still felt very flat in a good way: The insole is cushioned with nice arch support. The glossy finish made them feel more fashion-y and less traditionally equestrian (which I associate more with a light shine or matte leather). The wider shaft fell further from my calves, creating a more versatile silhouette that could be worn with shorts or with straight-leg jeans tucked in. I went with my normal women’s size 9 (the product description says the brand has updated its U.S. size grid) and it did feel like there was some sliding in the ankle or heel area, but wearing thicker socks seemed to help. Unfortunately, these don’t come in half-sizes, and if you are between two shoe sizes, Sézane says to choose the size above.

I didn’t realize how heavy the other riding boots I’d tried were until I put on the Dolce Vita Tywin. These knee-highs are sleek and lightweight, which made me feel like I was ready to saddle my imaginary mare and zip around a ring. They are rather minimalist and stripped down in design compared to other styles on this list. What sets them apart is the one-inch block heel, plus an outsole made of a lightweight recycled synthetic, rather than a heavy rubber or thick stacked wood. My only concern is that over time, the simple sole could flare up my tender plantar fascia — but during my initial wear testing, I didn’t notice any foot pain.

I’ve owned Frye’s signature Campus boots for about a year now, and they get better with every wear: more patinated, more formed to my foot, and more reason for why the style is much loved. Still, the $500 price tag is steep, so I decided to try the Quinn style, which is under $330 and has full-grain leather. I’m always in the mood for some gold hardware, and these have brassy D-rings and side zippers. The heel looks pretty minimal at first glance, but it’s actually about 1.4 inches thanks to a hidden internal wedge; I could immediately feel the slight lift. The shaft, or collar, is cut to be higher on the outside and lower on the inside, which is actually typical in real riding boots for outer protection and to prevent pinching inside the knee.

These nearly made the top spot, but the two-tone black-and-mahogany leather definitely makes these a more unexpected equestrian boot than one in a solid leather color. If that’s what you’re going for, the Quinn fits the bill — I know I’m still going to wear mine a ton this fall, but they may take more proper styling. For a more classic Frye riding boot, I’d opt for the Phoebe below.

In addition to suggesting the Quinn, Frye’s brand representative recommended I try the new pull-on Phoebe boots. These aren’t as glossy as the Sézane pair, but the soft leather and its pebblelike surface reads somewhere between lightly shiny and matte depending on the light. These have a curved shape at the top with the shaft rising higher on either side of the knee. I found the design gave room for my kneecap and really lengthened my leg. They have some western flair, which reminded me of my Staud Western Wally pair. Compared to the Quinn boot, which has a prominent D-ring, the only hardware on the Phoebe is two small buttons that sit on either side of the outer pull tabs. The sole felt super comfortable from the moment I first tried the Phoebe, and the outsole is made of lightweight EVA with a textured tread ideal for slick surfaces. There also seemed to be more wiggle room in the toe box and heel-cup area, but nothing that felt unstable or like my feet were sliding around.

I don’t know why I’m surprised that Lands’ End makes well-made boots. It’s been almost exactly two years since freelance contributor Erika Veurink wrote about how the brand’s solid quality and ability to ignore fast-moving trends means it flies under the radar and feels versatile and truly effortless. These boots are no exception. Made from smooth, matte leather, they have full-length interior zippers and a handy elastic that runs down the back shaft for extra stretch but is hardly noticeable. The low 1.25-inch heel combined with an EVA foam insole is incredibly comfortable. The outsole is rubber, which feels plenty durable for days when sidewalks are covered in salt and sleet. I guess my only complaint would be the silver hardware on the black leather (the brown rich-coffee leather has gold hardware). That said, I decided the hardware color shouldn’t be a deal-breaker when the boots are as comfortable as they are and come with an under $300 price tag (even less when they’re on sale).

entry.title: What Amy Grant Can’t Live Without
entry.summary: “I was coming out of one of the surgeries and I remember one of the nurses saying, ‘Look, her lipstick is still on!’”
entry.content:
If you’re like us, you’ve probably wondered what everyday stuff famous people add to their carts — like mascara or a sleep mask. We asked singer-songwriter Amy Grant — who released the deluxe edition of her album The Me That Remains earlier this month — about the snake boots, lip gloss, and breath mints she can’t live without.

My lips never chap because I put this stay-on lip color on there. And then also, it just stays on. You know, my job, I’m touching my mouth to a microphone all the time. It doesn’t smear. All kinds of companies make a stay-on, but I’ve always used Covergirl. And I always mix the colors together. I usually have on at least two or three colors.

In the last five years, I’ve had several unexpected surgeries. I was coming out of one of the surgeries — I think it might have been throat surgery because I had a growth nestled into my vocal cords. And I remember one of the nurses saying, “Look, her lipstick is still on!” And they were wheeling me into recovery! And I thought, Oh, I guess I put on Covergirl this morning.

I mean, unwanted hair is unwanted hair. I have a couple of unwanted hairs now growing out of my face. I’m almost 66. I’m like, What is up with this? But it could be anything, it could be Oh my gosh, I put on a sleeveless thing and I’d never even thought about checking my armpits. It’s the first sleeveless day of spring. I just always know where a razor is. I keep one in the glove box of my car. Legs don’t really bother me, but I’ve been through times of my life that I swam quite a bit. You got to do a little body maintenance if you’re going to come out in public in a bathing suit. You never know when that razor is going to be very essential. I tend to buy Venus, but anything works.

I’ve been a Crest toothpaste user since I was a kid. It’s familiar. But I’m fine if what’s available is not Crest. I sat next to a woman at a dinner party one time and she handed me two little packets of Unpaste tablets. She said, “I designed these for when you need to brush your teeth and there’s no water. And they take up no space.” And I enjoy camping, and a lot of times, I travel so much, I’m working out of a backpack. That would be my most recent non-Crest positive experience. I try to take care of my gums. And I like a vibrating-head toothbrush because you can do a really thorough job even if you’re not concentrating on it.

I have a farm. It’s not, like, a gentleman’s farm — it’s rough. It’s wild. And I’ll probably never live there, although I’ve spent many nights there. But there’s a lot of wildlife there, and we do have snakes. And so I have purchased these snake boots. I think mine are at least 25 years old. They’ve got Vibram soles, which is a great hiking-boot sole. I hike in these.

Most snake bites happen on the calf or ankle. So if you’ve got a good snake boot on, you’re just not going to get bit. The foot part is leather, but the stuff on the side is some kind of fabric that cannot be bitten through. I have seen rattlesnakes on our farm. Not so many, but I do love spending time outside, so snake boots are essential.

Well, I like that they don’t have sugar in them. They’ve got something, but my experience with Altoids is that sugar creates its own aftertaste. I’ll throw a bunch in my pocket, even if I don’t take the carrying case. And I love coffee, and so I’m always thinking, Oh my gosh, coffee doesn’t have a good breath shelf life! I like the taste of good breath, and I like those mints.

I love coffee being part of my morning ritual. I start the day off with an eight-to-nine-minute routine that’s all stretches and just normal ways that you would move. It always makes me smile, so I named it “Child’s Play.” But it’s a great way to start the day, and then coffee’s my reward for that.

I stress half-and-half. I’ve had a great cup of coffee, I’ve had some brilliantly brewed coffee, I’ve had bad hotel-room coffee that tastes like cardboard. But if you can add half-and-half to it, it improves the quality of anything and everything. If I’m going on a weekend trip, crazy as it sounds, I have a couple of little plastic bottles and I’ll actually take half-and-half in a backpack. You just never know, so that’s always in my bag.

I purchase Nespresso pods. I fell in love with that coffee maker because, well, for the last decade, my husband has played with the Eagles since Glenn Frey passed away. The caliber of hotels that the Eagles stay in is different than what I book on a work trip. I was like, Wow, this is what life looks like from the top! And every hotel had this Nespresso coffee maker, different versions, and they would have different-colored pods, and I was like, Oh my gosh, this is truly amazing. So over the last ten years, I’ve been through two or three different versions — I think most machines are sort of built with some degree of planned obsolescence. But I know the color of the pods I like, so I go, Oh, I’m going to get that one again.

Several people in the band that I’m playing with, the musicians and singers, and also guys in the crew, their ritual of coffee in the morning — I mean, there’s scales and they’re always finding their favorite bean of the month and the grind and the pour and everything, and I’m like, “Just hand me a Keurig, as long as there’s half-and-half.”

I write something every day. Because of the shape of my life, I don’t necessarily have a regular rhythm because I wake up in different places for days on end. But whether you’re making a list or doing some kind of a journal entry or writing a lyric, man, a pen with a good roll makes you want to keep writing. There were times in my life when I wrote a lot. I filled a spiral notebook in the late summer of 2022. I’d had a bike accident, and I had a brain bleed, and so I had several months that were very quiet. I couldn’t look at screens, I didn’t have my phone, I was waiting for my brain to heal so I could have a couple of surgeries for further repair from that wreck. I was writing to remember. I was trying to remember the names of everyone in my extended family. And I wrote with a pen, obviously, and I wrote in cursive because it does something different to your brain when you write in cursive. It’s a continuous thought, and I was welcome for any input that would help me on my healing journey. It’s funny — I filled that notebook, and I’ve never gone back to reread it. It doesn’t even matter, and at some point, I’m sure I’ll throw it in the trash, but that was the most intense relationship I’ve ever had with writing. And it was several months. I was really glad for every good rolling pen.

Sharpie actually has a great rolling-tip ink pen. If a hotel pen is good, I’ll write a little something. Right now, my pen box is filled with a lot of hotel pens. But I have a favorite. If it’s a level playing field, the one I always get is called Writon Gel 0.7. I buy them in bulk.

The red letters is a version of a New Testament. Some Bibles are made where all of the words of Jesus are red letters. I love to read. There are books that I’ve loved that I’ve read three or four times. But for me, I always return to the red letters. They mean different things at different times in life. There’s never been an account of anybody’s life that has captivated me the way the life of Jesus has. And I don’t understand it all — there are times I’ve been like, I don’t even know what this means! But who in the world has lived like that? That the only thing they ever did was good and true and kind and sacrificial. And, you know, in a time when women were property, he honored women. And he loved the outsider. And he just did good to everybody. To me, the whole world should at some point in life be curious to read the red letters because no human has lived that way. And I’m not proselytizing — I’m just like, if I had to read the words of anybody, these are mysterious and inspiring and life-giving. These are words that I want to read.

I inherited my grandmother’s cast-iron skillets. And I love going to antique stores or whatever junky-junk old stores, especially when I’m on the road. People are always getting rid of cast iron. And old cast iron — if you buy a new cast-iron skillet, it tends to have a grainier surface. But my grandmother’s, they are smooth. And it doesn’t matter how rusted a cast-iron skillet is, you can clean it up and condition it again and make it usable. To me, it’s a timeless, very useful piece of cookware. That’s the first thing I pull out when I’m going to cook anything. If you have cast iron that’s not precious — I have some sentimental pieces — I have a great apple-pie recipe that you make in a cast-iron skillet, and it’s lovely to be able to give the skillet and the pie. I have found some great skillets in whatever old shop is in a small town on Main Street. It’s fun to have something very specific that you’re looking for. And people have all kinds of specific things they’re looking for, but for me, it’s always cast iron.

entry.title: I Resisted the Ruti Pants for a Year. Now I Never Take Them Off.
entry.summary: Instagram made the On the Loose Work Pants look perfect. I was surprised to learn they actually are.
entry.content:
Never has the roller coaster of prospective consumption — the magnetic pull of targeted ads, the resentment of those ads, the obsessive research — hit me so hard as it did with the On the Loose Work Pants, a garment made by a Bay Area–based brand called Ruti. Somewhat unremarkable at first glance, the pants are cut in a slimmer-fit barrel leg that is ever-so-slightly cropped.

I first learned of these pants two summers ago, when they were recommended enthusiastically by an interior-design influencer I follow. Her appraisal didn’t read like sponcon — I don’t think it was — and it lit up a lot of regions in my brain. I was a 37-year-old, work-from-home mom of a toddler, desperate to look good (or good enough) and feel at ease without wasting precious time, money, or energy. This particular influencer assured me that the Ruti pants would solve all my problems: uncannily flattering and comfortable while also elegant and nicely tailored in a breezy, indestructible fabric. The On the Loose pants could actually be worn to a gentle yoga class then a lunch meeting; while feeding yogurt to my daughter at home and then boarding a flight. At no point would I ever feel overdressed or slovenly.

I signed up for Ruti’s text alerts and added the pants to my cart before getting distracted, and I briefly stopped thinking about them. They are, after all, a pretty forgettable garment: Made of nylon and spandex, they’re on the dressier end of the nebulous athleisure category and look like something Lululemon or Alo might make. The $249 price tag is high, but not high enough to qualify them as a status garment like those other viral $860 High Sport pants. In that world of quiet luxury, the Rutis are more like discreet comfort. Online, they look pretty indistinguishable from hundreds of barrel pants I’ve scrolled past over the years — just more catnip for millennial moms.

And yet they wouldn’t leave me alone. Once they came into my field of vision, the On the Loose Pants never left. There they were, in more targeted Instagram Stories and in banner ads on New York Times recipes. There they were, being recommended by influencers I follow on Instagram and TikTok, each of them posting enthusiastically. “Why did I wait so long to buy these?” They’d wonder, followed by a reassurance that these pants are, in fact, as good everyone says. The pants got so popular that they inspired a slew of dupes, including a pair by Old Navy and another one by Amazon.

Usually when I want something that’s been advertised to me, I can wait out the urge and it’ll slip from my mind. Not these pants — I couldn’t stop thinking about them. Were they a feat of aggressive marketing or something more? So I called Ruti Zisser, the former tech executive who started her eponymous label 2009. She launched the brand with a boutique in Palo Alto and clothes abiding by three strict principles: It must be cool, it must be flattering, it must be practical. “I designed this brand for women basically 35 and up,” Zisser said.

About a decade ago, she began refining a pair of pants that would eventually become the On the Loose. They were based on a pair of barrel legs she’d discovered at a store in Japan. “I’ve loved barrel-leg pants for ten years,” Zisser told me, but the Japanese pair were cut so wide that most women couldn’t pull them off. Zisser and Ruti’s then-designer took those Japanese pants and gradually slimmed them down until they were a more accessible silhouette, then hunted for the perfect fabric. An earlier version was launched under a different name and slowly refined each year. By 2025, they had the perfect cut and fabric locked in. “We looked for the fabric for years,” Zisser said, describing a lightweight but substantive blend that drapes well and is not remotely shiny. That’s “what makes it so special,” she added. “Now that we have it, it’s basically our secret.”

In 2019, during a more innocent time of online marketing, Ruti caused a minor stir by using facial-recognition technology in its boutiques. According to a report by the website Glossy, customers who walked into any of Ruti’s nine stores would have their faces scanned by a set of cameras. These photos would be stored and indexed in Ruti’s marketing database, and if the customer returned to a store, the information would go to sales associates to help pull sizes and recommend styles. When I asked her about the technology’s impact, Zisser was vague but noted that it helped grow in-store sales “massively.” “Retail with no technology is not going to work,” Zisser explained. “The idea that the company doesn’t have all that information is insane.”

When I asked Zisser about the strategy used to market the On the Loose pants, she was more coy. “We are a brand that doesn’t spend so much money on marketing,” she explained. In the early days of On the Loose, the team relied heavily on gifting to content creators, with the goal of getting “user-generated content,” which does not involve official sponsorships. “We didn’t want to pay for advertising, so we just gifted,” Zisser said. A lot of brands do this, but it doesn’t always lead to the next viral hit. Here, though, “people fell in love with the pants.”

Early boosters included small and mid-level content creators who were just on the cusp of middle age, like wardrobe stylist Becca Kahane and Nashville blogger Michelle Tomczak, who talked about the elegant practicality and versatility of the pants. But soon, their reach spread beyond the 35-plus crowd Zisser had always envisioned. “Right now, we’re finding out that a lot of younger women wear the pants,” Zisser said. “My daughter is 19, and she and her friends wear them.” By the end of last year, the On the Loose pants landed on the top-100 most-recommended list published by ShopMy, the website through which most content creators manage their affiliate links.

I made it a full year without buying them, which felt like an exercise in durational impulse control. This past summer, though, I met up with a friend who is younger than me and who has very good taste. She was in town from London, and when we hung out, my eyes were instantly drawn to her pants, which were sporty but elegant, loungey but equipped to do some serious summer schlepping. When I asked her where she got them, she explained that they were “some Instagram brand” and contorted her body to check the name on the tag. Ruti. Here were the On the Loose Work Pants in the flesh. She owned multiple pairs. “I never wear anything else,” she said a bit sheepishly.

With that vote of confidence, I pulled the trigger and purchased my own — the basic black. I also bought the $30 Amazon version as a sanity check. The Amazon pair, with its thick, crinkly fabric, smelled like chemicals and made me look like I was wearing a summer snowsuit. The Ruti version, on the other hand, made me feel like myself. The flat waistband across the front helped me seem put-together, while the elastic in the back was forgiving. I’ve never liked cropped pants, but the ultraslight crop here made me feel like I could wear any shoe without worrying about the hem.

And that was the theme of the On the Loose pants: They let me stop thinking about what I was wearing, which feels like the ultimate luxury. I am only a little bit ashamed to admit that I’ve worn them almost every single day over the last month.

entry.title: My Favorite Pen Is Cheap, Beautiful, and Writes Like a Dream
entry.summary: After amassing a trove of expensive fountain pens, I was surprised to find I loved using this gel pen the best.
entry.content:
For those of us who journal, draw, jot, and scribble, finding the perfect pen is a personal and sometimes lifelong endeavor. I have made many pen quests, delving deep into the veritable ink well of options and coming out with stained fingers and dashed hopes of the perfect tool. After amassing a trove of expensive fountain pens, I was surprised to find my absolute favorite daily writer in the Uniball Zento gel pen. It’s cheap, beautiful, and writes like a dream.

I’m no stranger to gel pens. They are a logical choice for someone like me who became frustrated with the maintenance and messiness of fountain pens. Although it remains true that nothing comes close to the feel of a fountain pen for pure writing bliss, you have to be willing to put up with refills, cleaning routines, ink mishaps, and smears. After a while, I got fed up. I just wanted something without all the fuss.

Despite the wide variety of gel pens and roller-ball pens out there, each with their own base of superfans, I never found the perfect fit for me. Some that promised smooth, deep, bold lines ended up stalling and skipping after only a couple of weeks of use (those would be the Pentel Energel line, Papermate Inkjoy, and Uniball Signo). Others were more reliable but felt too “sticky” with that classic ballpoint resistance (the Uniball Jetstream). Others seemed to check all the boxes but were sadly housed in a simply hideous form-factor that didn’t get me excited to use (the Pilot Precise V5 RT).

When I saw the Uniball Zento being hyped in stationery blogs and Instagram ads, I was skeptical of yet another overpromising pen. But I was immediately taken with its aesthetic. It’s friendly, modern, and dispenses with the typical dated marketing imagery. It even comes in tasteful colors as opposed to flashy metallics plastered with logos. The Zento has a smooth barrel, rounded at the end and sheathed in a grippy rubber that extends from the tip halfway up the length of the pen, smoothly transitioning to a velvety plastic. For us fidgeters, there are fewer protrusions to pick and pry, making it easier to keep the pen in one piece. It has a familiar push-button clicker and one of my favorite clips of all time. As someone who compulsively breaks off pen clips, the Zento’s lovely metal design is much harder to destroy than most.

The Zento was released in 2025 and was supposedly the result of years of development at Uniball. I’m not sure how much of that is marketing hype, but I do know the Zento writes beautifully. It glides smoothly across the page, leaving a bold, uniform line in its path. I can write fast without too much pressure and come away satisfied with consistent, dark strokes. My fast scribbly sketches are no problem for the Zento. The ink dries fast, so smudging is a rare occurrence, and it doesn’t bleed through most papers, even after some manic layering. You can get the Zento in .38-, .5-, or .7-mm thicknesses. I prefer the boldness of the .7-mm nib.

A pack of four Zento pens will run you about $6 on Amazon. They are widely available in various-size packs. If you fancy blue or red ink, those variations are available, though harder to find as cheap as the standard black. Other variations include the Zento Flow, which simply features a metallic bottom portion of the barrel, and the Zento Signature, which has a premium design with a postable cap (i.e., you can stick it on the other end of the pen while writing). These are in high demand and often marked up significantly when they’re in stock.

After years of babying precious fountain pens, the basic and budget nature of the standard Zento suits me perfectly. If I lose one (which I have and will), it’s not a big deal. I can toss it in a bag carelessly and still be confident that when I dig it back out I will be served with excellent feel and reliability. More than that, because of its considered aesthetic, it’s a pen that is always satisfying and a delight to use.

entry.title: 9 Things That Delighted Us Last Week: 10 Years of Toe Separators
entry.summary: Plus musician Rob Thomas’s Uniqlo sweatpants.
entry.content:
We write about hundreds of products each week. Here, in our version of the Sunday circular, we’ve plucked some of our recent favorites: expert-recommended essentials, life-changing stuff you didn’t know you needed, newly launched gizmos, and very good deals we uncovered while trawling through the vast online-shopping universe — including a potty trainer that can do it all, a worth-it J.Crew men’s cotton crewneck, and our kitchen writer’s new favorite mallet.

“The Agnès B. snap cardigan has always been a workhorse of my wardrobe,” says contributor Leah Finnegan. Then she found out she was pregnant, and shortly after the cardigan shrunk in a laundry fiasco. In search of a dupe, she tried out six of the most similar cotton-fleece snap-button cardigans she could find, and this $88 one by Skims came out on top. Its “classic cardigan shape with a tucked waist is both flattering and comfortable,” especially on Finnegan’s growing belly, and it won’t be a big deal if her baby throws up on it.

This week, the Strategist site celebrated its tenth birthday. Senior writer Dominique Pariso took us on a walk down memory lane by rounding up the top-ten products that define the Strategist. Among them are the “squishy, ladderlike toe separators” lead editor Lauren Levy ends her days with for fear of “bunions, hammertoes, and any and all podiatric-related issues,” she says. She’s not the only one who keeps the “jellyish, aqua-blue toe-stretchers” in her nightstand; Kelly Rowland and Simon Rex do too.

Senior writer Emma Wartzman has used wine bottles, rolling pins — anything but a mallet — to flatten her cutlets. That changed after visiting her family this summer, where she first tried this mallet. She loved it so much, her mom sent her one soon after. The rounded stainless-steel handle makes for a balanced hold, and the head’s flat side is Wartzman’s favorite, as it gives her the most control over where she’s hitting. Though she uses it largely for meats, it’s also great for “smashing aromatics like garlic and ginger,” breaking down nuts and chocolate for baking, and crushing ice for drinks.

Over the past two years, senior writer Liza Corsillo has noticed a shift in training–potty releases. More and more of them now resemble a “mega potty,” a cross between a traditional mini-toilet and an attachment you can place on your regular toilet seat that’s meant to grow with your child. With the help of her son, she tested seven. Jool Baby’s was a standout — it’s an affordable floor potty, step stool, potty-training seat, and urinal in one. “What I love about it most of all is that it can be used as a urinal,” she says, “which has helped my son understand the logistics of peeing while standing up without getting pee all over the place.”

We first spoke with musician Rob Thomas in 2022 for our “Celebrity Shopping” series. Writer Amelia Jerden recently caught up with him about all the new things he can’t live without, including the women’s sweatpants he first saw on his son. Now he can’t get enough of them: “I walk around the house, and they feel luxurious. First they became, like, These are my favorite going-to-the-grocery-store pants. And then they became, like, Well, these are my favorite going-to-the-airport pants. How far of a radius I would leave my home in sweatpants just got bigger and bigger and bigger when I started buying these.”

“Maybe it’s an Asian Mom thing, but I believe most shoes should always be worn with socks,” says senior writer Lauren Ro. Hue’s sock liners are her favorites, so she decided to test the brand’s “do-they-even-qualify-as-socks” toe toppers and covers. These liners were the perfect invisible counterpart to her go-to cotton ones, “keeping dainty shoes dainty and my bunioned feet happy” in the stiff opera shoes and ballet flats she normally wears sockless. They’re thin and slippery like tights but stay put all night thanks to a silicone grip on the heel that has the added bonus of preventing blisters.

Senior writer Michael Zhao was reminded of J.Crew’s reliably designed and constructed knits after stopping by the Men’s Shop in Noho to try on all 15 sweaters in the store. In a sea of cashmere and wools, this cotton sweater made his list of absolute favorites. “The heavyweight cotton knit drapes so luxuriously,” he says. This year’s version forgoes the style’s previous raglan sleeve for more elevated-looking standard shoulder seams (Zhao’s preference). Available in 11 often-on-sale colorways, “why not get a bit more for your money?”

In search of this year’s birthday present to herself, a new fall bag, contributor Sari Botton tried out 16 cross-body bags, hoping to find one that’s gentle on her arthritic joints. Madewell’s richly colored, lightweight leather bag scratches Botton’s Bottega Veneta itch at a fraction of the cost. “It’s a good size — a bit bigger than the average going-out-at-night bag and a bit more compact than your average everyday bag, meaning I won’t be tempted to pack it to the gills,” she says.

Synthetic fleeces were introduced as more durable, economical, and easy-to-care-for alternatives to wool, but the research has shaped a different story, according to writer Katherine Gillespie. “Synthetic fleece sheds higher amounts of nonbiodegradable microplastic fibers into waterways than other synthetic materials when laundered,” she says. In response to this and other fears surrounding wearing polyester, brands have designed plastic-free fleeces like this L.L.Bean one, which is made of a majority-wool blend that’s soft and machine-washable.

entry.title: The 10 Very Best Electric Toothbrushes
entry.summary: Including rotating, oscillating, and sonic toothbrushes.
entry.content:
As the Strategist’s personal-hygiene writer, I find brushing my teeth is much more enjoyable with an electric toothbrush. Plus, it’s nice knowing I’m always getting a thorough brush thanks to quadrant timers and pressure sensors. Buying an electric toothbrush doesn’t have to be expensive, either: There are plenty of budget-friendly options out there as well as souped-up models for anyone obsessed with tracking their health stats.

Many dentists think electric toothbrushes have a slight edge over manual ones because they can be better at reducing plaque, gingivitis, and the risk of gum recession since they lessen the force we put into cleaning our teeth and gums. When shopping for an electric toothbrush, start with a model that has an ADA Seal of Acceptance to make sure it’s safe and effective when used as directed. After that, you shouldn’t really stress — at least not when it comes to picking among the dentist-approved electric options. Sonya Krasilnikov, a dentist and co-founder of Dental House, says, “Choosing between Sonicare and Oral-B is like picking between a Mercedes and a BMW. It’s mostly personal preference.” Since the differences between them can be so subtle, to put together this guide, I brushed my own teeth with some of the dentist-recommended picks below and tested features like pressure sensors, two-minute quadrant timers, and more.

Updated on October 23, 2026
Our favorite electric toothbrushes have been updated with the latest availability. We’ve added the Suri Core as a less-expensive sustainable toothbrush option.

Electric toothbrushes tend to fall into three camps: rotating, oscillating, and sonic. “Rotating or rotary toothbrushes have small circular heads that rotate back and forth to clean each tooth, and there’s sonic toothbrushes that have vibrating brush heads that move the bristles side to side at really high speeds, sometimes up to frequencies of 50,000 movements per minute,” says Dr. Cooper. Sometimes you will hear oscillating and rotating used interchangeably because they both refer to the actual movement of the bristles — unlike sonic which refers to the vibration of bristles — but rotating indicates movement in a circle while oscillating refers to a side to side motion. Some dentists say that one isn’t necessarily better than the other, while others appreciate the power of sonic slightly more. Dentist Sharon Huang of Les Belles NYC explains that sonic toothbrushes use a sonic wave to dislodge debris all on its own, which she likes because it requires less force to get the job done. “The rotation mechanism, you actually have to touch the tooth and it’s rotating and it’s helping you clean it,” she says. “The sonic toothbrush has a sonic wave. So if you’re in the vicinity, and you’re not even touching your tooth, it’s supposed to be dislodging bacteria.” The sweet spot is a toothbrush that does it all, but orthodontist Janet Stoess-Allen, says that because teeth are curved, “rotating heads are more effective in getting to all sides of them.”

“Hard-bristled toothbrushes are wonderful if you’re going to clean the grout from your bathroom tile, but they’re not for use in the mouth,” says Messina, who explains that harder bristles can damage gums and enamel. Every expert we spoke with said a soft-bristle brush was the way to go in all cases, but especially if you have sensitive teeth and gums.

Brushing too hard can be just as damaging as brushing with too hard of bristles, which is why dentist Inna Chern likes brushes with pressure sensors that beep or stop moving when you’re being too aggressive to “eliminate the possibility of overzealous brushing.” A pressure sensor shouldn’t make or break your decision when deciding on what brush to go with, but Huang does think it’s a good idea for people switching from a manual brushes to an electric one for the first time who might be used to be putting some extra umph behind their strokes, which electric toothbrushes don’t require.

Built-in timers are more standard than pressure sensors and a little more essential. Leonard Umanoff of Brooklyn-based LuxDen, recommends toothbrushes that have a built-in timer, as this helps make sure you’re brushing long enough to adequately get rid of plaque. Some will just run for the recommended two minutes, while others have a quadrant timer that will alert every 30 seconds when it’s time to move to the next quadrant of your mouth.

The consensus is that the smaller the brush head the better. Chern says it’s a good pick “if your mouth is on the smaller side or you have gagging issues.” It also makes it easier to reach your molars, a hard to clean area that people often miss, according to Dentist Hemita Klose of West Village Dental Studio. There are a few cases where a larger head might be better. Orthodontist Heather Kunen reminds us that a toothbrush is only as good as it’s operator, so for brushers who are less meticulous about moving a small brush around every corner of each tooth, they’ll benefit from a broader head.

Toothbrush bristles become worn and frayed over time, making them less effective at cleaning your teeth. It’s recommended that they’re replaced every three months. Here, I’ve linked to replacement toothbrush heads made by the brand and broken down the cost per head.

While the Oral-B Pro 1000 is a pretty basic and affordable entry-level electric toothbrush (high-end models could run you upwards of $300), it has all the main features dentists recommend. That’s why I bought this toothbrush myself back in 2020 when I first upgraded from a manual one. I have since upgraded again — more on that below — but revisited the Pro 1000 for testing. In the past three months, my teeth feel as squeaky clean as they do with my souped-up toothbrush. While I miss the tracking capabilities of my current model, all of the features that make brushing with an electric toothbrush easier and more effective are here: The built-in two-minute quadrant timer vibrates every 30 seconds, and the pressure sensor stops the pulsation if I’m brushing too hard. Oral-B brushes are known for their small round heads, which allow me to brush around each tooth.

Cosmetic dentist Lana Rozenberg likes that Oral-B brushes generally “have more features” and are “more advanced than the others.” They have a slight edge over competing popular electric toothbrushes because they rotate, oscillate, and pulsate (or vibrate), combining all three technologies. This brush can rotate 44,000 times per minute, which dentist Jonathan Levine says causes “a lot of disruption of plaque.” According to the Oral-B website, all of its round toothbrush heads rotate 45 degrees to the right and back to 45 degrees to the left, as well as oscillate back and forth.

I upgraded from my Oral-B Pro 1000 to its newer iO Series toothbrush about a year ago. Off the bat, it’s a much sleeker model, with its OLED display on the brush handle and magnetic charging stand, but its souped-up features stand out most. Like the Pro 1000, it combines rotating, oscillating, and sonic technology, plus a two-minute quadrant timer to make sure you’re brushing the right amount of time. Rather than one mode, it comes with seven: daily clean, gum care, sensitive, super-sensitive, whitening, intense, and tongue clean. I personally use the two-minute daily-clean setting twice a day, which leaves my teeth feeling squeaky clean. And the less-intense 30-second tongue-clean mode got me in the habit of brushing my tongue more regularly (I try to use it at least every other day). I now have fresher breath than when I was brushing my teeth and swishing around mouthwash. The toothbrush’s pressure sensor is more advanced, too. A light at the top of the brush turns red if you’re brushing too hard, white if you’re not brushing hard enough, and green if you’re brushing just right. What I found most helpful, however, is the app it uses to track brushing habits. The toothbrush uses an AI technology called 3D Tracking to show real-time feedback on the app: a rendering of your teeth progressively gets whiter until it tells you that section is fully cleaned. Over time, you can see your progress on the app too. It tells you which spots you frequently miss, so you can easily change bad brushing habits. While it is pricey, I think it’s worth a splurge if you’re wanting a high-tech option.

Our best-overall pick is an Oral-B, but for those who want to go with the other major player in the space, Sonicare, this is your best option. Sonicare brushes are distinguishable from Oral-B brushes mainly by the brush head. Sonicare’s heads are large and flat compared to Oral-B’s small round brushes, and they’re long-lasting, according to Wellspring Dental dentist Mandy Nebel, who prefers Sonicare over other brands. This specific model — one of two from the brand accepted by the ADA — is a more entry-level Sonicare. When I tested it out for myself, I found it a lot less noisy than the Oral-B best-overall option. I think this is because of how the brush head moves. It doesn’t rotate and instead moves side to side and uses more of an ultrasonic vibrational energy to disrupt plaque and tartar, aiding in the removal of gingivitis-causing, bacteria-holding compounds. Even though it moves differently, I found my teeth feeling just as clean as when I brushed with the Oral-B Pro 1000. Similarly, this Sonicare has a quadrant timer, pressure sensor, and soft bristles. A couple of bonuses: It has a light that tells you when to replace the head and a protective brush cap. The main reason that it’s not the best overall is the larger brush head, which may not work for most people, but other than that, it’s an excellent option for about $50.

For better or worse, your toothbrush doubles as bathroom décor, so having one you won’t mind looking at every day is a good idea. Last year, Quip released its newest model — the Rev Oscillating Toothbrush — and its design reminds me of the now-discontinued Goby toothbrush, which used to hold the “nicest-looking” title. It’s much more modern-looking and sleeker than your typical Oral-B or Sonicare, but it isn’t just nice to look at. It has everything I want in an electric toothbrush: a small brush head that oscillates, soft bristles, a pressure sensor, and a two-minute quadrant timer. I’ve tested it for about two months now and can say its cleaning holds up compared to the Oral-B Pro 1000 and Sonicare 41000. I’d say its gentle setting is the softest of the three models, so this could be a better option for those with sensitive teeth or gums. Senior editor Crystal Martin uses the Quip almost exclusively on the gentle setting, and says it is soothing compared to other electric toothbrushes and still gets the job done. To boot, the price of the Quip is right in line with those basic models at around $50.

Brush movement: Sonic | Soft bristles: Yes | Pressure sensor: Yes | Timer: Yes | Brush head size: Large | Replacement heads: Three for $19 ($6 each)

The brand Suri launched in 2022 with its sustainable sonic electric toothbrush. The sustainability aspect piqued my interest, since the body’s made of aluminum and steel and bristles made of cornstarch and castor oil. When I tried the first version, it unfortunately stopped working after about a month of testing. But, Suri has since released the 2.0, which I’ve been testing for three months now, and it’s held up wonderfully.

It has two cleaning modes, a pressure sensor, and a two-minute quadrant timer, which make brushing easy. The bristles are soft, but my teeth feel squeaky clean afterward, and the brush itself is incredibly lightweight and sleek. My colleague Brenley Goertzen, who’s also been testing it out, echoed these sentiments. We both also noticed how quiet Suri is compared to other toothbrushes (her old toothbrush was a Sonicare and I’ve tested ones from both Sonicare and Oral-B). On top of that, this comes with a convenient travel case with UV-cleaning capabilities. Because of my limited counter space, I typically store mine in the case on a daily basis and in my bathroom drawer, but I’ve also thrown it in my Dopp bag on trips without an issue.

Last month, Suri also released a basic electric toothbrush at just $75, which is a little over half the cost of its Pro model with the case included. Like the Pro, the Core toothbrush features a two-minute quadrant brushing timer and a pressure sensor, and it’s made from the same sustainable materials. It’s also quiet and effective at brushing away plaque. What you don’t get with the Core is the option of a travel case. But it does come with a magnetic mirror mount and charging port. This is a great entry-level electric toothbrush for anyone concerned about cutting down on household plastic. If you travel frequently, though, I’d recommend going with the Pro version.

If you’re shopping for an electric toothbrush and a water flosser, consider this two-in-one model that combines the best of both devices. It has three functions — brushing, flossing, and both — and two brush speeds. Compared to regular flossing, water flossing can be easier for those with limited mobility or certain dental work, like braces or implants. And it even “removes the harmful bacteria and debris deep between teeth and below the gumline that traditional brushing and dental floss can’t reach,” says Dr. Jacqueline Fulop-Goodling, an orthodontist at New York’s Dr. Smiles. But while it shouldn’t replace traditional flossing, it’s the next best thing, says Rabinovich, who uses one herself and recommends it to patients. She even says that after using it, her mouth feels like “I just had my hygienist go at it.”

Brush movement: Sonic | Soft bristles: Yes | Pressure sensor: Yes | Timer: Yes | Brush-head size: Large | Replacement heads: Three for $25 ($8 each)

This two-in-one flosser and toothbrush system recommended by Dr. Elisa Mello, owner of NYC Smile Design, is about $50 cheaper than the Fusion Professional model above. You won’t get the same convenience of water flossing and brushing at the same time, but if you’re looking for an all-in-one device where you have options to do both, this is a great affordable model. The brush has three sonic modes (clean, whiten, and massage for gum stimulation) and three speeds, so it actually has more brushing options than the Fusion. The flosser itself has ten different pressure settings, ranging from 10 to 100 psi, and the 22-ounce tank holds enough water to run for 90 seconds. And while the toothbrush has a two-minute quadrant timer, the flosser does not.

Generally, you’ll want to wait to introduce kids to electric toothbrushes since toddlers’ gums may be too tender for bristles, Rabinovich tells us. Usually, kids’ electric toothbrushes are marketed for ages 3 and up, but Rabinovich recommends them for those older than 5. If you’re having trouble acclimating your kid to an electric toothbrush, Dr. Rashmi Ambewadikar of Astoria Smiles Pediatric Dentistry recommends starting with front teeth and moving toward the back to avoid gagging and the feeling of vibration on the tongue, and brushing small sections at a time to give them breaks. Steven C. Cohen of Livingston Smiles and Rabinovich both advise going with a brush with their favorite character or cartoons. “Are they in a Disney Princess or PAW Patrol stage? Kids are more likely to use a toothbrush with their favorite characters on it,” Rabinovich says. Cohen approves of Oral-B’s collection of kids’ brushes. This one is rechargeable and has a sensitive brush head with soft bristles and a built-in timer.

Quip, as mentioned above, is known for making sleek-looking, minimalist toothbrushes at an affordable price. Rabinovich’s kids use the brand’s kids’ toothbrush, which “does offer some ultrasonic vibration, but it’s not overwhelming” for teeth that are still growing. I’ve tried the brand’s regular toothbrush in the past and can say it’s much gentler than the other ones I’ve tried on this list, but my teeth always felt clean after using it. Rabinovich says that’s because its soft bristles are surrounded by rubber massagers, which are gentler on tender gums with loose and erupting teeth. “And the subscription service for replacement heads and batteries means one less thing for me to remember to do as a parent,” Rabinovich adds. Dr. Ambewadikar also recommends Quip’s brushes for kids because its smaller handle is easier to grip. Another major benefit I found is that it doesn’t require a charging base and frees up counter space — something families sharing a bathroom might appreciate. Bonus: It comes in four bright, kid-friendly colors: blue, pink, purple, and green.
